entries.title: USS Abraham Lincoln Arrives at Thailand Port After Nine Months at Sea
entries.summary: The aircraft carrier is en route to America after deployment to the Middle East.
entries.content:
By Sakchai Lalit and Anton L. Delgado

LAEM CHABANG, Thailand — The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived in eastern Thailand early Wednesday after its grueling deployment in the Middle East.

Associated Press journalists watched the Lincoln, which is carrying about 5,000 service members, approach Laem Chabang port in Chonburi province shortly after the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. sailed passed the area.

The ship had been supporting the U.S. war against Iran. Its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days. Concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products.

The usually Asia-based U.S.S. George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

Many of the service members are expected to make a visit to Pattaya, a nearby popular beach town. Thai officials have said the Lincoln’s stop would be for rest and recovery before returning to its U.S. base.

Pattaya officials said they welcomed the visit and the potential boost to the local economy. Authorities said they are stepping up security to ensure a smooth visit.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Beatty Seeks Release of Sealed Kennedy Center Renovation Documents
entries.summary: The plans were issued just two days before the board convened to shutter the facility, the Tuesday court filing says.
entries.content:
Rep. Joyce Beatty wants a federal judge to unseal two documents the Trump administration used to justify its latest attempt to engrave the president’s name onto the Kennedy Center.

In a motion filed Tuesday, Beatty’s attorneys say the records — a building plan and a five-slide PowerPoint presentation — served as the only pretext for what they called a “rushed effort” by a mostly Trump-appointed board of trustees to shutter the facility and circumvent an earlier court ruling ordering the president’s name be scrubbed from the building’s facade.

“As before, these new documents were ‘light-on-details,’ contained no meaningful ‘cost-benefit analysis of the closure,’ and constituted a ‘stacked deck,’” the motion states.

The Ohio Democrat’s attorneys said the Trump administration intentionally obscured the documents from the public without ever filing a formal motion to seal or explaining to the court why the records must remain secret. The court should at minimum agree to release the documents with limited redactions obscuring only sensitive security or financial details, they wrote.

“This is a case of enormous public interest about public officials’ maintenance of a public memorial to a slain President,” the filing says. “Defendants cannot simply allude to their ‘general interest’ in keeping their documents ‘out of the public eye,’ because doing so would seal everything under the sun in a case of enormous public significance.”

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled against the administration in May, and ordered that all signage and references to the “Trump Kennedy Center” be removed from the building.

The board voted on Aug. 13 to shut the Kennedy Center down in a second round of the legal fight to put Trump’s name on the building. Justice Department lawyers representing the center say the president’s name could go up as soon as next week, though Beatty’s attorneys are seeking to temporarily block the change.

Beatty, an ex officio member of the board of trustees, said the two documents were created just two days before the board convened to shutter the facility, mirroring the board’s previous “hasty attempt.” The construction plan for a full facility closure did not include a thorough cost-benefit analysis, the filing says, while the short PowerPoint was “riddled with internal inconsistencies.”

Government lawyers and officials have warned that the center could deteriorate⁠ into an unsafe structure and eventually face demolition if the renovation is halted.

The administration opposes the motion, according to Beatty’s filing. Representatives for the DOJ and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Democrats Think Seth Moulton's Failures Are a Warning for 2028 Candidates
entries.summary: How much do voters care about age over ideas?
entries.content:
Each time he’s tried to climb the political ladder beyond his seat in the House of Representatives, Rep. Seth Moulton has pitched himself as someone who can usher in the Democratic Party’s next generation.

And each time — including in Tuesday’s Massachusetts Senate Democratic primary, in which voters picked Sen. Ed Markey over Moulton — voters have rejected him.

Moulton, who arrived in Congress by beating a nine-term incumbent, was once part of a rising class of young(ish) Democrats styling themselves as the next generation leaders of their party. He was part of a failed effort in 2018 to oust Nancy Pelosi as the top Democrat in the House Democratic Caucus, arguing that “Our party is changing, our country is changing and our leadership should change, too.” His bid for president in 2020 — which kicked off with, “The greatest generation saved our country from tyranny. It's time for our generation to step up and do the same” — fell short.

In his campaign against Markey, Moulton declared, “I’m running against the senator’s decision, after 50 years in Washington, to run for another term at age 80.”

Now, Moulton’s failed Senate bid in one of the last major Democratic Party showdowns of the cycle is a warning to the party as Democrats begin to assemble for what’s expected to be a messy 2028 presidential race. The lesson from his collection of unsuccessful campaigns, other Democrats say, is that it’s not enough to just position yourself as the poster child of a new generation of leadership — winning candidates need to have something actually new to say. 

“The moment that we're in right now isn't just about electing young people, but it's about electing people who have new and big ideas,” said Rep. Maxwell Frost of Florida, the youngest member of Congress at age 29 and a rising star in the party.

In some ways, the Moulton-Markey primary in a state as blue as Massachusetts turned the party’s biggest intraparty feuds on their head. The younger candidate in this primary was more moderate than the older incumbent. Even during an insurgent wave that has led to at least seven other Democratic incumbents losing their seats, the 80-year-old Markey won reelection in part because of his progressive bona fides — despite a gaffe during a debate that showed his spotty understanding of AI platforms.

Moulton, whose campaign didn’t respond to a request for comment, fell short of convincing voters, but he also couldn’t convince much of the party to back him: Markey gained momentum in the final weeks of the campaign as he notched endorsements from Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and longtime ally Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Sanders, a kingmaker for the left wing who has his own track record of running competitive if ultimately unsuccessful presidential campaigns, was frequently named in interviews as an example of someone older being able to energize the party.

“This is the same reason that Bernie keeps winning reelection, even though he's a little bit older,” said Charles Hughes, chair of the College Democrats of Massachusetts, which endorsed Markey. “As long as the candidate shows that they're capable of fighting for those progressive causes and fighting for the issues that young people care about, I think age is a secondary factor.”

These generational questions are already following Democrats into the 2028 presidential race. Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, 39, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, 44, Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, both 53, are all considered to be among the youngest possible contenders.

“These candidates who run on change will have to prove that they actually are making change in order to do that, not just showing that they are a younger face necessarily,” said David Hogg, founder of Leaders We Deserve, which works to elect young Democrats.

Moulton’s loss reflects how the party has evolved since former President Joe Biden’s aborted reelection campaign. Youth is still important for young Democrats, but they say they want more than just a number.

“Age to me isn't really the big thing,” said Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer who beat Rep. Diana DeGette, 69, in Colorado’s 1st District this summer. “It's about, does your platform actually speak to what this new generation of politics is demanding?”

Even if Moulton wasn’t successful at running as a change agent, there are Democrats who think there’s a case to be made for candidates trying to run on changing the status quo, regardless of their age or how many times they’ve tried it.

“The system is still very stale, and so even a guy like Seth is still a younger candidate in relation to what people see in Chuck Schumer, for example,” said Tim Ryan, a former lawmaker from Ohio who unsuccessfully ran against Pelosi in 2016 for House minority leader.

“People want a new set of eyeballs on the problem,” he went on.

Moulton on Tuesday signaled he planned on continuing to play a similar role in the future.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary," he said in a statement after the race was called. "I will continue to push the Democratic Party – and our country – to look towards the future.”

–
Editor’s Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Christa Dutton

entries.title: Democrats Are Fuming at Two Moderates Who Helped Bail Out Republicans
entries.summary: Party leadership has asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take up the issue.
entries.content:
Two moderate Democrats bailed out House Republicans from an embarrassing loss on the floor thanks to a revolt from House conservatives, leaving their Democratic colleagues fuming.

Reps. Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington state voted alongside Republicans to move forward with debate on several bills, including a provision to condemn socialism that Republicans are expected to tout on the campaign trail. Their “yes” votes caught Democratic leadership completely by surprise.

Members of Democratic leadership said in a statement Tuesday night that they plan to take quick action against the pair. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar said they have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules — which recommends changes for how the party handles legislative priorities — to take up the issue.

“The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust,” they wrote. “It is an action that necessitates a serious response.” 

Jeffries told reporters earlier in the day that he did not know that those Democrats, whose votes were decisive in advancing the procedural measure, were planning to vote with Republicans.

A Democratic leadership aide told reporters that leadership does not whip votes on procedural rules as minority members. It’s extremely rare for a member to cross party lines to support the opposition’s agenda.

"I am fucking livid," another House Democratic aide, who requested anonymity to speak freely, told NOTUS.

Golden is not running for reelection, while Gluesenkamp Perez is defending her seat in a race the Cook Political Report has deemed a “toss up.” Golden told reporters that he voted in favor of the rule in order to advance a bill he sponsored, the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act, that was part of the rule package.

Golden added that it was not necessary to inform leadership because “everyone in all of Congress knew exactly what I would do this week for Maine fishermen.”

“The idea that anyone represents their constituents, came here, introduces a bill to support that constituency, would do anything but vote for it is fucking nuts,” Golden said. “Could you imagine going home to your constituents and being like, ‘I was trying to help you, but I had to vote no'?”

Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee, said he is “very disappointed” in the pair, adding that “this makes us look like them,” referring to Republicans, who frequently squabble with each other.

Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-California) told NOTUS that she similarly does not support members of the caucus voting with Republicans on procedural measures.

“No, obviously, I voted no,” Jacobs said when asked if she thinks Democrats should be crossing the aisle on rule votes. “I think unity is incredibly important in the Democratic caucus.”

Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-Illinois), a longtime member, told NOTUS that Democrats should be working together.

“I don’t know what it was meant to mean, but I’m not for that,” Schakowsky said. “They should not have done that, I think.”

Rep. Sanford Bishop (D-Georgia) said that although representatives can vote the way they feel best helps their constituents, he was disappointed to see Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez break with leadership on a rule vote.

“I hate that we had the opportunity to win that vote for the American people, and that we had some people on the team that couldn't go along with it,” Bishop said. “At the end of the day, each of us has to live with our own conscience, and we've got to let our conscience guide us in terms of what our constituents would ask of us.”

Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas), who is also in a “toss up” race, told NOTUS that while his district is different from many Democrats hold across the country, he has a “very open relationship” with leadership. He noted that he would have shared how he planned to vote in a similar situation.

“I tell them what I’m going to do ahead of time. I don’t hide from what I’m going to do,” Gonzalez said. “If you like it, fine. If not, we care about the people in our district.”

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who earlier in the day told Politico she was disappointed in the two members and “never had that problem” with a rule vote in her time as speaker, told NOTUS that she ultimately suspected the rule might have advanced even without Democrats’ help.

“The Republicans probably had a couple of votes up their sleeve anyways,” Pelosi said.

But members of Republican leadership also signaled to reporters on Tuesday that they were not aware Democrats would cross the aisle to support the rule. In a press conference just after the vote, Speaker Mike Johnson did a victory lap.

“Many of you thought that would not happen today, but we passed a rule to continue business this week,” Johnson said. “Republicans are here to work. We have a lot more left to do.”

This story was updated to include a statement from Democratic leadership.

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area Over Labor Day Weekend
entries.summary: DC Tap Fest, DC JazzFest and a (literal) circus on the National Mall.
entries.content:
Thursday

Live! At The Library
The Library of Congress, Jefferson Building, 10 First Street SE, 5 to 8 p.m., free

We’ll take Celebrity Podcast Tapings for free, Ken. This week’s Live! At The Library, features Jeopardy! host Ken Jennings and his podcaster pal John Roderick. The duo will record an episode of “The Omnibus Project” in the Coolidge Auditorium and devote their banter to books, objects and artifacts in the library’s collection. Meanwhile, in the Great Hall, banjo player John Bullard will pick a mix of bluegrass and classical music. Stroll while enjoying drinks and snacks, or check out the reading room, which is normally reserved for researchers. (Pro tip: If tickets are sold out, try again Thursday morning, when the Library of Congress releases a fresh block.)

“Garbo” at GALA Hispanic Theatre
3333 14th Street NW, 8 p.m. $22

GALA Hispanic Theatre opens its 2026/2027 season with a world premiere play about Catalan actor Juan Pujol García (a.k.a. “Garbo”) who took on the role of double agent during World War II. His escapades included collecting wages from the Nazis for nonexistent fellow spies and helping to convince the Germans that the Allies would invade not at Normandy, but at Pas-de-Calais. In Spanish with English subtitles. Friday’s performance is a discounted preview; the play continues through Sept. 27.

More to explore: British glam rocker Adam Ant plays the Filene Center at Wolf Trap.

Friday

DC Tap Fest All-Star Concert at The Westin Washington
1400 M Street NW, 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. (two shows), $45

DMV tap dance doyennes Chloé and Maud Arnold return to curate four days of classes, performances and jam sessions. Friday night’s All-Star Concert features the Syncopated Ladies, the Arnold sisters’ touring ensemble that has performed on “So You Think You Can Dance,” “The Late Late Show” and more, plus shared stages with a host of celebrities, including Mariah Carey. Luke Spring, an Ashburn native who was on Broadway before he turned 10, also performs.  

Bernstein’s Mass, Mount Vernon Place United Methodist Church
900 Massachusetts Avenue NW, 7 p.m., free

Chamber opera company the INSeries and singers from 13 area choral groups combine forces to offer a requiem for the Kennedy Center. The Gay Men’s Chorus of Washington, Georgetown Chorale and Handel Choir of Baltimore are among those sending volunteers to perform the piece Leonard Bernstein composed to memorialize John F. Kennedy Jr. and celebrate the center’s opening in 1971. Heather Adelsberger of the Georgetown Chorale conducts and Timothy Nelson, artistic director of the INSeries, provides stage direction. (The concert repeats on Saturday.)

More to explore: First Friday at Community Forklift in Edmonston.

Saturday

DC JazzFest at Arena Stage and The Wharf
Saturday and Sunday, times and costs vary

DC JazzFest takes over the Waterfront neighborhood this week with performances on more than a dozen stages. Highlights include the free outdoor DC Jazz Bops kids concert (both Saturday and Sunday at 11 a.m.), sets sponsored by EU embassies at Union Stage and the Pearl Street Warehouse, and the DCJazzPrix, a competition for emerging ensembles. Block out some time to explore the website in advance, because some shows, including Saturday’s Arena Stage headliner featuring Dee Dee Bridgewater, are only open to festival passholders.

Circus Arts Conservatory at the Smithsonian
Arts and Industries Building and National Museum of American History, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., free

The Smithsonian’s annual Folklife Festival may have been bounced off the National Mall by the Great American State Fair, but events have still happened, mostly indoors in a scaled back form, throughout the summer. This weekend, the Smithsonian celebrates circus arts with three days of performances, demonstrations and workshops at the Arts and Industries Building (a.k.a. The Castle) and the Museum of American History. Bring the kids for hula-hoop and juggling workshops, short performances featuring the Sailor Circus Academy from Sarasota, Florida, and (we are not making this up) read-aloud storytime with clowns.

More to explore: Whiskey tasting and distillery tour at Mount Vernon.

Sunday

So many museum exhibitions are closing
Various locations around the National Mall 

As summer ends, so do a host of museum exhibitions. At the Hirshhorn, Labor Day weekend marks the closing of “Basquiat x Banksy,” an exploration of contemporary street art. At the Renwick, you have one last chance to see crop art and more at “State Fairs: Growing American Craft.” And at the Museum of the Bible, sample pages from the 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls are on display for their final few days.

The Hot Lanes at Fort Hunt
Pavilion A, 8999 Fort Hunt Road, Alexandria, 7 p.m., free

If getting the kids (or older adults) downtown seems like a bridge too far, the final Fort Hunt Sunday night concert of the season may be a great alternative. The Hot Lanes, a local 16-piece ensemble inspired by Wynton Marsalis and his Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, close out this series held on National Park Service property just north of Mount Vernon.

More to explore: The National Symphony’s free Labor Day Concert at DAR Constitution Hall.
entries.author: Rebecca Ritzel

entries.title: Taking Aim
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Sept. 2, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

D.C.’s restrictive gun laws have come under legal assault over the past 18 months, leaving local officials concerned that the city’s persistent gun violence could get worse.

There have been legal challenges to D.C.’s ban on assault rifles and high-capacity magazines, and to the law prohibiting people with felony convictions from possessing guns, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports.

Many of those challenges stem from a 2022 Supreme Court decision that made it harder for jurisdictions like D.C. to justify their restrictions on guns. The Bruen ruling, as it’s known, says limits on gun possession must have some equivalent in American history or tradition. If not, they’re unconstitutional.

D.C.’s ban on high-capacity magazines has been litigated, and this year a panel of judges on the D.C. Court of Appeals ruled that it was unconstitutional. (That ruling is on hold pending a further appeal.)

The Trump administration has been leading the charge against some of D.C.’s gun laws. It backed the challenge to the high-capacity magazine ban, and separately sued the city over its prohibition on AR-15 assault rifles.

Defense attorneys are now fighting to overturn D.C.’s felon-in-possession law, saying it's unconstitutional. The office of U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro, which prosecutes most violent crime in the city, told NOTUS that she will “always fight to keep illegal firearms out of the hands of dangerous felons.”

Some of these new legal challenges are already making their way to the Supreme Court. Later this year, the justices will consider whether outright bans on assault weapons are unconstitutional.

“The weakening of our gun laws is only going to make public safety more difficult,” D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson told NOTUS.

DEEP DIVE

Janeese Lewis George made Anacostia’s Union Temple Baptist Church the first stop of her campaign's citywide listening tour on Tuesday night, signaling a shift from winning votes to gathering community feedback. NOTUS’ Michael Brice-Saddler reports that Lewis George said starting in Ward 8 was an intentional effort to prioritize a historically marginalized part of the city.

The packed crowd — which included Ward 8 council member Trayon White — split into breakout groups to discuss localized issues ranging from homeownership to public safety and education.

Lewis George said she plans to use these ward-by-ward meetings to build a focused administration agenda, setting the tone for her transition by asking the room: “How do we get from words to plans to actions to accountability? That’s what this is about.”




FROM THE DISTRICT

East Potomac golf course (7008x4672, AR: 1.50)
All’s quiet at East Potomac Park. Months ago, President Donald Trump declared that major renovations of the island park’s golf course would begin on Sept. 1. But NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad reports that it was a sleepy Tuesday at East Potomac. On the day some locals had long dreaded, the area was mostly quiet. A few people fished. A pack of cyclists zipped through bike lanes. A couple enjoyed a mini-golf date.

A few backhoes were staged in a parking lot, but nobody was there to operate them. After a few days of tree removal last week, a Maryland-based tree care company was seen driving around the perimeter of the park. Otherwise, life went on as normal.

There are now fewer National Guard troops in D.C., reports WUSA9. As of Monday, the count stood at 3,865, down 663 from the week before. That decrease is probably linked to the end of summer events for America’s 250th anniversary. Though there are fewer troops, their presence is expected to continue into 2029. As NOTUS recently reported, D.C. residents are conflicted about the Guard’s presence.

He drove a 10-foot-tall homemade guillotine around the U.S. Capitol in the bed of his pickup truck, but Philan Le didn’t expect to get criminally charged for the stunt, The Washington Post reports.

Check, please. Washingtonian magazine resurrected its guide to the D.C. area’s “Best Cheap Eats” for the first time since 2019, listing 60 selections available for under $25.





FROM VIRGINIA

Some Northern Virginia homeowners, sick of living in the data center capital of the world, are moving elsewhere, Axios D.C. reports.





FROM MARYLAND

A deadly wrong-way crash in Montgomery County last weekend has put county police on the defensive about disbanding their impaired driving enforcement unit, WJLA reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For quiz masters: Live! At the Library featuring Ken Jennings at the Library of Congress, Thursday.

For jazz enthusiasts: DC JazzFest at Arena Stage and The Wharf, Saturday and Sunday.

For people who like free things: The National Symphony’s free Labor Day Concert at DAR Constitution Hall, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Commanders training camp has come to a close and suddenly Week 1 is around the corner. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson looks back on everything we learned about this year’s team since camp opened July 29. From the much-needed arrival of Stefon Diggs to the recent spate of injuries, there was no shortage of drama in Ashburn.

D.C.’s new Major League Volleyball team officially has a name: D.C. Flight. The Washington Business Journal reports that the women’s indoor volleyball franchise will begin its inaugural season in January, with plans to play home games at a “major performing arts venue in D.C.”

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Braves, 1:05 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Lillian Bautista/NOTUS.

entries.title: Old Man-achusetts
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Senior Night in Massachusetts. Why Abdul El-Sayed apologized. Democrats in disarray on Capitol Hill. Interior Department fears. DOJ election monitoring plans. And: How to run against an independent.

Take our five-minute survey! Help us make a better NOTUS newsletter.





THE LATEST

Age is just a number: Two big takeaways from the Democratic primaries in Massachusetts last night: the polls were right, for once, and there are still no easy ways to summarize what has happened inside the party this year. Safe-blue House seats with very little chance of being flipped by Republicans were held by older incumbents against younger, progressive-leaning challengers — though both Reps. Richard Neal and Stephen Lynch had more of a race than they’re used to. Contrast that with other safely blue places in New York or Colorado or etc., where incumbents could not catch a break.

In the Senate primary, incumbent Ed Markey dispatched a challenge from the younger Rep. Seth Moulton early in the night, suggesting he’s one older Democrat who remains clued in to what it takes to win in his state. Moulton came into Congress by beating a nine-term incumbent, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton writes, and has repeatedly pitched himself as a leader for a new generation. The problem is voters seem to really not care for Moulton, no matter how old or young he is. There’s a lesson here for would-be presidents in 2028, Democrats told Christa: They need to bring new ideas and not just a more recent DOB.

Of note: “Sens. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) are the remaining members of Congress who were in office during Gerald Ford’s presidency,” the Washington Examiner’s David Mark wrote on X.

More on NOTUS: U.S. Strikes Targets in Iran and Tehran Fires Back | Trump Nominates Hung Cao for Navy Secretary | Florida Becomes First State to Remove Flock Cameras From State Roads | Trump’s Call to ‘Let Data Reign’ Clashes with Republicans’ Caution

Open tabs: Case against suspect in Charlie Kirk’s killing can proceed to trial (CNN) | Putin Pledges Increased Strikes in Ukraine and Support for Iran (NYT)





From Michigan


Abdul El-Sayed talks to NOTUS: It’s been a few weeks since El-Sayed narrowly won the bitter primary to become Michigan Democrats’ Senate nominee and he is still struggling to unite a fractured Democratic electorate. In an interview with our Alex Roarty for the On NOTUS podcast out today, El-Sayed explained his recent in-depth apology for his response in March to an attack on a Michigan synagogue. He condemned the attack at the time but also tried to make a larger political point about Middle East violence. (“Hurt people hurt people,” he said of the attacker, who had lost family in an Israeli strike.) He now says that approach was a mistake.

“I wanted to make sure that folks understood that the attempt to offer a broader context in a moment so close to an attack like that was ill-timed. It was ill-suited for the broader goal I had, which is to say when a community is attacked, it’s wrong,” El-Sayed told NOTUS. “There’s plenty of opportunity to talk about how things are interconnected, but not in the acute moment of pain.”

Is this the approach that finally puts the primary in the past? Polls continue to show a very tight race with Republican nominee Mike Rogers, and plenty of Democrats still consider El-Sayed to be a liability. But if he can make unifying moves like the apology stick, he can move on to the kind of general election he promised voters.

One that sounds like this: “A beta his whole life,” is how El-Sayed described Rogers.

From the Hill


Big mad: “I am fucking livid,” said a House Democratic aide, who requested anonymity to speak freely, and then did, after two moderate Democrats, Reps. Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington state, bailed out House Republicans from an embarrassing loss on the floor. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the caucus was “blindsided” by the pair’s support of a GOP rule, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra and Kadia Goba report, and Democratic leaders are now looking at how to discipline the defectors whose actions they called a “significant breach of trust.”

Golden didn’t hold back when asked to explain his vote: “The idea that anyone represents their constituents, came here, introduces a bill to support that constituency, would do anything but vote for it is fucking nuts. Could you imagine going home to your constituents and being like, ‘I was trying to help you, but I had to vote no’?”

More on NOTUS: House Republicans Pass Resolution Denouncing Socialism | House Votes to Censure Chuck Edwards Over Harassment Allegations

From Interior


Parks & Uncertainty: Current and former Interior Department staffers fear a major overhaul ahead after National Park Service brass called an unusual in-person meeting with superintendents of all the country’s national parks later this month, NOTUS’ Anna Kramer and Eric Katz report. “Attendance is mandatory and expected. We will use this time to discuss agency priorities, our FY 2027 outlook, and other matters important to the work ahead,” an NPS official wrote. The meeting comes right after reassignments affecting some of Interior’s top experts.

From the DOJ


All-call: The leader of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has one request for her staff: become election monitors. It appears to be part of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s plan to send an unprecedented 1,000 monitors across the country to polling locations for the midterm elections. In an email obtained by NOTUS’ Eric Katz and Derek Hawkins, Dhillon said she was looking for staff to volunteer and work polling places across the country on Election Day or in a call center in Washington.

“I’m writing to encourage each of you to sign up and join us in this effort,” Dhillon wrote. While the DOJ has repeatedly sent election monitors to voting places, this new request carries significance amid the Trump administration’s efforts to oversee how voting in states is conducted.





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

After the vote to censure Rep. Chuck Edwards yesterday, Dana Milbank argues the only thing Mike Johnson’s House is good at doing is wrongdoing.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: D.C.’s Strict Gun Laws Are Being Put to the Test, by Martin Austermuhle

What to Do in the D.C. Area Over Labor Day Weekend, by Rebecca Ritzel

Sports desk: 10 Things We Learned From Commanders Training Camp, by Martenzie Johnson





NEW ON NOTUS

Labeling the unlabeled: Independent candidates for Senate have popped up across the red-state map this cycle, trying to give voters an alternative where Democrats can barely fantasize about being competitive. Republicans think they have a pretty handy way to deal with this, NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández reports — calling them Democrats. Independents, meanwhile, welcome the challenge.

That’s how it’s playing out in Nebraska, where Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts is vying against independent Dan Osborn.

“Our approach is straightforward: expose the truth about Dan Osborn’s far-left views and the Democrat infrastructure behind his campaign,” Ricketts’ deputy campaign manager, Max Oberg, told NOTUS in a statement.

More: Media Site Asks Judge to Block Trump From Posting Official News on Truth Social, by Gavin J. Quinton

Milo Yiannopoulos Says He’s ‘Ashamed’ of Supporting Trump After Deportation, by Torrie Herrington

New Emails Show Bovino Was Under Investigation Prior to His Retirement, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Interior Department Staff Are Fearing a Major Agency Shakeup
entries.summary: Former National Park superintendents are cautioning the Interior’s top leadership against another reorganization.
entries.content:
With limited insight into the Trump administration’s plans for the Interior Department, and recent reassignments affecting some of the agency’s top experts, current and former staff are seeing signs of a dramatic shakeup on the horizon.

In the latest example, the superintendents of all of the country’s national parks have been called to unusual in-person meetings with National Park Service political leadership later this month, scheduled for just a few weeks before the end of the government fiscal year.

“Attendance is mandatory and expected. We will use this time to discuss agency priorities, our FY 2027 outlook, and other matters important to the work ahead,” wrote Frank Lands, the deputy director of operations for NPS, in communication to park leaders reviewed by NOTUS.

The meetings are all scheduled for the week of Sept. 14 at each regional office around the country, with agency leadership suggesting they may travel to attend each meeting.

The timing has alarmed current park service staff and former superintendents, who told NOTUS that Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has until now largely prohibited travel for senior park service staff. They are anticipating a major reorganization of the agency that they fear could resurrect previously abandoned efforts to cut or consolidate NPS offices focused on science, wildlife monitoring and culture. Staff in other bureaus throughout the department echoed those concerns to NOTUS in recent days.

Employees said the coordinated rollout elevated their levels of panic. Individual park and headquarters staff — in D.C. and in Colorado — told NOTUS they have been left out of the discussions entirely.

These fears have reached former park service leaders. A coalition of 20 former park superintendents, including former leaders of Yosemite, Grand Canyon and Acadia, wrote to Burgum on Wednesday, warning that any reorganization of the park service would “make it all the more difficult” for the agency to serve the needs of the parks.

“Requiring attendance at a last minute meeting at the end of the fiscal year is unusual in this current environment, to say the least. And it is concerning, given the consolidation that has occurred since January 2025, and the efforts at reorganization we have seen at DOI and throughout other federal agencies,” the superintendents wrote in the letter, organized by the Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks and shared exclusively with NOTUS.

“Reorganizations can be useful when they are carefully planned, transparent and driven by the mission. They can also cause enormous damage when they are rushed through from the top, without understanding how a complex organization actually functions,” they wrote.

The Interior Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In August, Interior reassigned about 30 of its most senior civil servants — known as senior executive service employees — to new roles, requiring many people to move into new jobs with limited relationship to their background and expertise, NOTUS previously reported. Those who were reassigned were given two weeks to accept the change or resign.

Those reassignments did not include regional staff, though some employees said they expect that to change in the coming weeks.

Interior has already reorganized its workforce once under Burgum’s tenure.

In 2025, the agency moved people specialized in human resources, information technology, contracting and other related areas from bureaus such as the park service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service into a centralized organization within Burgum’s office.

While the agency carried out that reorganization, it simultaneously lost more than 10,000 employees across its many bureaus, largely through deferred resignation and retirement incentive programs designed by the Trump administration. The National Park Service has lost almost one-quarter of the permanent, full-time employees it had at the beginning of the second Trump administration, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management’s staffing database.

Federal spending law requires the Interior Department to get permission from Congress before it reorganizes its bureaus. The Republican leaders of the committees with jurisdiction over the department did not respond to requests for comment.
entries.author: Anna Kramer, Eric Katz

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Explains Why He Apologized for His Statement on a Synagogue Attack
entries.summary: The Democratic Senate nominee said he wasn’t trying to “score political points” when he apologized recently for a statement he made after a terrorist attack on a synagogue.
entries.content:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, said he is “deeply committed to the safety of the Jewish community” after apologizing for past comments linking a terrorist attack on a synagogue earlier this year to a greater cycle of violence.

“I felt the need to apologize, and apologize clearly and directly, for the pain that I might have caused,” El-Sayed said on the latest episode of the On NOTUS podcast. “We can disagree agreeably that my commitment to Palestinian self-determination does not come at the cost of Jewish safety, and where my words obfuscated that, I needed to correct that.”

Earlier this year, a man crashed a car into a synagogue in a Detroit suburb and began shooting, injuring a security guard, before being killed in a shoot-out. The attacker was identified as a naturalized U.S. citizen from Lebanon who had lost relatives in an Israeli airstrike in his native country a week before.

In a video condemning the attack, El-Sayed said that “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle.”

El-Sayed told NOTUS that he apologized for that statement, as it may have unintentionally seemed like he was justifying the attack.

“I wanted to make sure that folks understood that the attempt to offer a broader context in a moment so close to an attack like that was ill-timed, it was ill-suited for for the broader goal I had, which is to say when a community is attacked, it's wrong,” El-Sayed said. “There's plenty of opportunity to talk about how things are interconnected, but not in the acute moment of pain.”

El-Sayed’s apology comes as he is trying to unite the party behind his campaign amid criticism for his association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

“The reason I issued the apology wasn't to score political points,” El-Sayed said. “The reason I issued an apology is because I don't want to cause people pain.”

In an interview published in August with The Atlantic, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said she was “concerned” that El-Sayed still stood by his comments on the synagogue attack.

“What does that mean for American Jews moving forward if you can rationalize what’s happening in a war in the Middle East on attacks on your own people here in the state of Michigan?” Nessel said.

El-Sayed told NOTUS that he has not talked to Nessel since his apology, but is looking forward to speaking with her.

Democrats, such as Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, have criticized El-Sayed over his views on the Israeli government, but El-Sayed said there is room for disagreement within the party.

“The Democratic Party, as we always say, is a big tent,” El-Sayed said. “I respect my fellow Democrats who deeply disagree with me on this issue, and it is on us to make that argument to voters, and voters are gonna decide who they want to nominate and who they want to elect accordingly.”

El-Sayed was targeted with millions in outside spending from the powerful American Israel Public Affairs Committee in his primary campaign against Rep. Haley Stevens, and said he expects more of the same in the general election against Republican nominee Mike Rogers.

“Mike Rogers is going to bring huge amounts of outside money, largely funded by exactly the same people who funded the outside spending against me in the primary,” El-Sayed said. “He is going to try to make this race about everything except for the fact that you can't afford your groceries, you can't afford your home, you're worried about whether or not your kids are gonna get priced out of extracurricular activities like sports.”

Rogers has ramped up efforts to win over Jewish Democrats in the state, seizing on El-Sayed’s relationship with Piker and El-Sayed’s views on the Israeli government. El-Sayed, meanwhile, has been attacking Rogers regarding his relationship with President Donald Trump.

“I think Michiganders understand that [Rogers] is not a leader,” El-Sayed said. “He's been a beta his whole life. He's a guy who shows up to laugh extra loud at the alphas’ jokes. And that's what he does with Donald Trump, right?”



On NOTUS is a weekly podcast where NOTUS reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here.
entries.author: Alex Roarty, Ed Demaria

entries.title: 10 Things We Learned From Commanders Training Camp
entries.summary: Stefon Diggs rejuvenated the receivers room, injuries spoiled the summer and Jayden Daniels showed he’s still got it.
entries.content:
Following a 41-3 beatdown against the Ravens in Friday’s preseason finale, there are more questions than ever about what this Commanders season will look like.

One game doesn’t negate three months of practice, but it can highlight the issues a team is facing. For Washington, it’s clear the interior line isn’t up to snuff and the run defense leaks yardage like a spigot.

But there have been some positive strides since June. The receivers room is deep. The run game has improved. The front seven is disruptive. It’s not all bad.

Here are the 10 most important things we’ve learned about this Commanders team over the last few months:

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The receivers room struggled early. 

From the first days of training camp, it was clear that this team’s weakness was at receiver. The wideouts not named Terry McLaurin consistently struggled to get separation, leading to the quarterbacks holding onto the ball too long or throwing passes away. “We shake [hands] with guys after practice — I didn't really wanna shake up with anybody because we got beat,” McLaurin said after the second day of camp. “But at the end of the day, we're still brothers.”

The group’s lackluster showing eventually led to Adam Peters making a late signing.

Stefon Diggs’ arrival was a game changer. 

Isn’t it amazing how quickly opinions can change when a former All-Pro walks through the door? Every criticism of the receivers room seemed to evaporate the second Diggs stepped on the field Aug. 7. With his quickness and route-running, Diggs quickly became one of Jayden Daniels’ favorite targets in practice. We have yet to see what Diggs will actually look like in this offense — he played only three snaps in the preseason with no targets — but his arrival immediately improved the vibe of the team. That is until …

The offensive line fell apart. 

The offensive line came into camp as one of Washington's strengths. The unit returned four starters, and the fifth lineman, center Nick Allegretti, started the final two games of the 2025 season. But within one day of Diggs’ first practice, All-Pro left tackle Laremy Tunsil tore a triceps during a one-on-one drill. Less than two weeks later, Allegretti reaggravated a calf strain that had sidelined him early in camp. Brandon Coleman and Julian Good-Jones filled in at tackle and center, respectively. While Coleman, who was the team’s starting left tackle in 2024, seamlessly subbed in for Tunsil, Good-Jones struggled. The converted guard had issues snapping the ball and identifying defensive coverages, leading to sacks and run stuffs. Eventually, he was one of 34 players released on Sunday, though he was signed to the practice squad a day later.

But the injuries to Tunsil and Allegretti were just the beginning.

Jer'Zhan Newton AP - 26220040830441 (5340x3560, AR: 1.50)
So. Many. Injuries.

Late in camp, players began dropping like flies. Cornerback Trey Amos, linebackers Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson, defensive tackles Daron Payne, Tim Settle and Jer’Zhan Newton and running backs Bill Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White all missed multiple practices in the final weeks. Settle was the only one of that group who played in the preseason. Amos, Newton and Tunsil were all placed on injured lists, meaning they will sit for a minimum of four weeks.

Jayden Daniels is still that dude. 

Washington’s star quarterback faced a fair amount of restrictions in the preseason. In three snaps against the Lions, he handed off, was pressured into a throw away and sacked. But throughout camp the former rookie of the year looked poised, in command of the offense and still capable of dotting an “i” with his accuracy. He worked more under center than he has in his professional and collegiate careers, and his coaches have raved about how he has made that adjustment.

Bill Croskey-Merritt made his case.

Croskey-Merritt had about as well of a rookie season as can be expected of a seventh-round draft pick, posting a team-high 805 rushing yards and eight rushing touchdowns. But inconsistency and fumbles got him sent to the bench in the second half of the year. At the beginning of camp, coach Dan Quinn said he wanted to see more explosiveness and pass-catching production from the 25-year-old, and Croskey-Merritt provided that, even after the team signed receiving back White in the offseason as a third-down option. He made multiple difficult catches in camp, and when given the room by the line he hit gaps with speed and power. After missing a few weeks with a lower-body injury, Croskey-Merritt returned to practice on Tuesday.

Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson can give this team an edge. 

One of the reasons for the early skepticism around the offense was the pressure and penetration free-agent signees Oweh and Chaisson were creating in practice. Daniels and co. could barely get plays off because of how quickly the two edge rushers were making their way into the backfield. The only problem? Neither Oweh nor Chaisson has practiced since Aug. 12.

Sonny Styles AP - 26214719942040 (4546x3031, AR: 1.50)
Sonny Styles is still a work in progress. 

Having a positive opinion about Styles feels like raving about a restaurant to a friend, only to eat the food together and it’s just OK. The rookie linebacker spent all summer attacking run gaps and blanketing pass-catchers in practice, but when preseason games started the No. 7 overall pick didn’t look otherworldly. He didn’t immediately pass the eye test like other rookies have, including Tampa Bay’s Rueben Bain Jr. But Quinn can vouch for the early hype: “You guys have seen a lot more,” he said to reporters. “What I’ve seen at practice, you feel speed and playmaking ability to get to spots.”

Daronte Jones and David Blough faced growing pains. 

The two first-time coordinators created a lot of excitement in Washington when they were hired in January. Blough promised an explosive offense while Jones emphasized versatile and bespoke looks from his unit. While the preseason isn’t a barometer for how a team will produce, it can identify some weaknesses. The offense has faced protection issues and couldn’t get the run game going against Detroit or Baltimore. While the defense forced the kind of turnovers it lacked last season, the run defense allowed 160 yards a game, which would have ranked dead last in 2025. The saving grace is that the play calls used in preseason don’t always stick around for the regular season.

Something changed in the last two weeks. 

As Week 1 gets closer, it’s hard to ignore that whatever high Washington had going when they manhandled the Dolphins in mid-August has since dissipated. Part of that is due to all the injuries, but there's been a noticeable vibe shift regardless of who is on the field. Mental mistakes (turnovers, missed assignments, penalties) started to mount against the Lions, which led to Quinn stating the team was in “disarray.” And rather than learn from those mistakes, the Commanders were embarrassed by the Ravens in joint practice and the preseason finale a week later.
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Here’s How Republicans Are Running Campaigns Against Independent Candidates
entries.summary: A set of independent candidates is holding the Democratic Party at arm’s length. Republicans want to close that gap.
entries.content:
Republicans have a simple strategy for how to campaign against a slate of independent candidates running for Senate seats in red states: Take every opportunity to tie them to Democrats.

In Nebraska, South Dakota, Idaho and Montana, Republican Senate candidates are running against independents who have held the Democratic Party at arm’s length in order to make competitive runs. These are states where Democratic candidates have flopped in recent years.

Now Democrats are making the case that the independents — who they hope would caucus with their party, even as some of them have said they would not — stand a chance of defeating Republicans because of the current political environment.

“If the Democrats are calling me a Republican, and the Republicans are calling me a Democrat, I'm doing something right. So that's what I'm going with,” Brian Bengs, the independent running against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds in South Dakota, told NOTUS.

Republicans, however, believe the Democratic Party’s brand is noxious enough that they can effectively beat the independent candidates just by continuing to point out how Democrats are embracing them.

That’s how it’s playing out in Nebraska, where Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts is vying against independent Dan Osborn.

“Our approach is straightforward: expose the truth about Dan Osborn’s far-left views and the Democrat infrastructure behind his campaign,” Ricketts’ deputy campaign manager, Max Oberg, told NOTUS in a statement.

“[Democrats] know their brand is so toxic in these states that they're just going to try to put a false label on progressive candidates,” Oberg added.

Republicans are pointing out that some Democrats, like Cindy Burbank in Nebraska, David Roth in Idaho and Julian Beaudion in South Dakota, dropped out of their races to allow the independent candidates in their states the opportunity to consolidate voting blocs.

“There were two Democrat candidates in the race, and now there is one,” Sen. James Risch of Idaho told the Idaho State Journal in a statement, after Roth dropped out of the race to pave the way for independent candidate Todd Achilles. “Idaho remains one of the most Republican states in the nation, and I am proud to consistently deliver conservative votes for our state.”

The Democratic nominee in Montana did not withdraw despite mounting calls to drop out to allow a two-way race between the Republican candidate and independent Seth Bodnar.

The Republican campaigns have also pointed to some of the independents’ presence on ActBlue, a Democratic fundraising platform; Osborn, Bengs and Bodnar have all used it to raise money. On its site, ActBlue says it allows independent candidates on a “case-by-case basis” if they meet criteria the platform has set up.

Osborn has raised more than $5.7 million as of June 30, Federal Election Commission records show. At that point during his 2024 run against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer, in which he ran as an independent, Osborn had raised around $1.6 million. The boost in fundraising suggests growing interest in his race this cycle since he came within 7 percentage points of Fischer two years ago.

Bengs has raised more than $780,000 as an independent as of June 30 — an approximately $630,000 jump from what he raised in the same period in 2022, when he ran as a Democrat against now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune, according to FEC records.

“Bengs is out there using ActBlue and the Democrat machine to raise money, which should also tell everyone that he's a Democrat,” Rob Skjonsberg, a senior campaign adviser to Rounds, told NOTUS.

Still, most of the Republicans have outraised their opponents by millions. As of June, 30 Ricketts raised more than $11.4 million; Risch more than $4 million; and Rounds more than $4.5 million.

Republicans are leaning on referring to the independents as democratic socialists and associating them with the views of progressives running elsewhere, calling them “fake independents.” It’s reflective of their broader playbook against Democratic candidates.

“Dan Osborn, Brian Bengs, Todd Achilles, and Seth Bodnar would work in lockstep with the toxic socialist Democrats to enact their woke agenda and raise taxes for American working families,” Bernadette Breslin, who serves as national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee — Senate Republicans’ campaign arm — told NOTUS in a statement.

Democrats would have to flip a net of four seats in order to take control of the Senate.

Osborn, a navy veteran running to unseat Ricketts in Nebraska, is seen by political analysts as having the best shot of the independents. Although he has the endorsement of labor groups often associated with Democrats such as the United Auto Workers union, he also supports cutting federal spending.

In April, the Cook Political Report moved the Nebraska Senate race from solid Republican to likely Republican.

“If voters are convinced that this is a politician who is not going to be tethered to either party in a state like Nebraska and a year like 2026, yeah, Dan Osborn has a real shot,” Jim Kessler, the executive vice president for policy at Third Way, a “center left” think tank, told NOTUS.

Candidates like Osborn are making sure to keep their distance from Democrats. Although Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb said on X the party supported Osborn, he told CNN on Aug. 23 he planned “on remaining an independent.”

Osborn’s campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment.

“The reason that Dan Osborn and this independent movement has started was because Dan Osborn ran against [Sen.] Deb Fischer two years ago and got closer than anybody thought he would as an independent,” Mary Jane Truemper, the chair of the Nebraska Republican Party, told NOTUS.

Kurt Alme, Montana’s Republican candidate, has followed similar talking points to other Republicans. Breitbart News Network reported he called Bodnar a “Democrat in disguise.”

“I’m running for Senate as an Independent because Washington is broken, and Party bosses in DC are too busy fighting each other while families in our state face higher costs and fewer opportunities,” Bodnar told NOTUS in a statement.

Bengs and Achilles have considerably lower chances of pulling off an upset, Larry Sabato, a political analyst and director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, told NOTUS. But they have been targeted by Republican campaigns in nearly identical ways.

Both independent candidates have past connections to the Democratic Party. Bengs ran as a Democrat in 2022 and Achilles was elected to the Idaho state House as a Democrat in 2024. Both candidates told NOTUS they plan to join the Senate as independents and, while they acknowledge their past Democratic affiliations, Bengs and Achilles said they plan to caucus as independents.

Still, those commitments haven’t changed the Republican playbook against them.

“Our strategy is simple: tell the truth about Todd Achilles. He's a liberal Democrat masquerading as an 'independent' and his record makes this clear,” Marc Kilmer, Risch’s campaign manager, told NOTUS in a statement.
entries.author: Raymond Fernández

entries.title: Trump’s Call to ‘Let Data Reign’ Clashes with Republicans’ Caution
entries.summary: Many Republican candidates are running on pledges to pause new data centers, but the president’s position undermines that message.
entries.content:
First it was beef. Then it was new tariffs. Now it’s data centers.

President Donald Trump’s recent policy moves are making life difficult for Republicans, many of whom fear the series of economic positions could cost them control of Congress in November’s midterms.

Trump’s love letter to data centers this week undercut efforts by Republican candidates in battleground states to align themselves with a growing bipartisan backlash against new construction of the resource-intensive projects. His remark that communities that oppose data centers are destined to become “backwards and poor” landed like a thud on Capitol Hill and on the campaign trail.

“I guess I’m backwards and poor,” Tennessee Rep. Tim Burchett told a reporter for the outlet MeidasTouch on Monday, suggesting that new data centers ought to be built on military installations. “We need more local control. Go a little slower to get there a little faster.”

Freshman Rep. Rob Bresnahan, who represents a high-profile swing seat in Pennsylvania, told NOTUS he disagrees with the president on the matter.

“It’s something we have a different perspective on,” Bresnahan said, adding that he wants to ensure approved developments provide a benefit to the community.

“I have a piece of legislation called ‘Local Control Protections Act,’ which does exactly what the name insinuates. It empowers local communities and allows those decisions to be made at the local level. … We're about local control,” he said.

Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, who represents a deeply conservative district, appeared to criticize Trump’s position: “New directive from the leader: MAGA is required to support all Data Centers, no questions asked,” he wrote on X.

Data centers have become a major political issue as voters grow increasingly weary of their impact on the energy grid, utility bills and water resources. While most elected Republicans continue to cheerlead construction of new facilities, touting that they create jobs, GOP candidates in tough races have embraced restrictions on the industry, including moratoriums on new facilities and requirements that data centers cover the cost of electricity bills.

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, for example, has called for a one-year pause on new data centers. In Texas, where state Attorney General Ken Paxton is running for Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking reelection, both Republicans are also pushing to pause new data center projects, even though Abbott initially promoted Texas as a hub for the industry and offered tax incentives. In Pennsylvania, state treasurer and Republican gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity has called for an indefinite pause on new data center development. In Wisconsin, Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, has called for ending state subsidies for data centers.

“Tom Tiffany’s position has always been clear: Local communities must have the final say, and no new data centers should be built in Wisconsin without strong standards to protect our farmland, water, environment and ratepayers,” a Tiffany campaign spokesperson told NOTUS.

Nevertheless, Trump’s strong endorsement of data centers is handing their Democratic opponents a fresh line of attack.

“Make no mistake — this is Mike Rogers' position on data centers,” Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed wrote online. “He's got up to $2.6 million invested in companies cashing in on the data center boom, all while Michiganders watch their utility bills soar.”

The campaigns of Rogers, Paxton, Abbott and Garrity did not respond to a request for comment.

One Republican gubernatorial candidate did push back on Trump’s call to “let Data reign.”

“President Trump and I don’t see eye to eye on this issue,” wrote Darren Bailey, the nominee in Illinois. “As I travel across Illinois, I hear the same concerns: massive data centers are threatening farmland, straining our power grid and driving up costs. My position is clear: Illinois families and communities come first.”

Other Republicans suggested Trump’s historically poor approval ratings pose a bigger challenge for the party in this year’s midterm elections, rather than the issue of data center construction.

“I think Trump is right on the issue, despite the clumsiness with which he said it. The next 50 years could rest on the next five regarding AI,” Republican strategist Doug Heye told NOTUS. “But, I don't think it has much of an impact, where Trump's approval rating definitely does.”

Conservative radio host Erick Erickson, meanwhile, said on his show Monday that Trump stood up for data centers “probably in the least helpful way possible.” Erickson, who’s based in Georgia, praised Vice President JD Vance for taking a “far more nuanced approach.”

Vance expressed some sympathy for skeptics of the facilities while traveling Monday to Michigan, a state where communities have also pushed back against data centers.

“I think probably 99% of the backlash to data centers has come in areas where building a data center means higher utilities and higher electricity for the people on the ground,” Vance said.

He added that data centers “should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don’t think the data centers are that controversial. It’s when the utility bills get so much higher; that’s when it’s a real problem.”

Polls show deep distrust in data centers. In a Fox News survey conducted in July, 70% of respondents expressed opposition to the construction of a data center in their area, including 60% of Republicans and 76% of Democrats.

Former Georgia Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene was dismissive of the president’s position in a post on X: “Good luck winning the midterms now that MAGA means mass data centers, flock cameras and the surveillance state, protecting the Epstein class, and the never ending Iran War!!”

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), a prominent AI critic who led calls for a federal moratorium on data center construction last year, said Americans have “every right to be concerned” about them.

“They understand that data centers are destroying local environments and that these out-of-control technologies will likely eliminate tens of millions of jobs, eviscerate our privacy, negatively impact the mental health of our children, radically alter how we as human beings relate to each other, undermine our democracy and threaten the very future of humanity,” Sanders wrote in a post responding to Trump on Monday.
entries.author: Igor Bobic

entries.title: D.C.'s Strict Gun Laws Are Being Put to the Test
entries.summary: Recent cases have challenged prohibitions on assault rifles, high-capacity magazines and felons owning guns.
entries.content:
In June 2025, Lorenzo Redman was sentenced to 18 months in a D.C. prison after he was convicted of possessing a gun as a felon. His public defender filed an appeal.

But that appeal wasn’t based on a procedural mistake or legal technicality. Rather, his attorney argued that in disarming felons, D.C. has been violating the Second Amendment.

Redman’s case — one of two pending before the D.C. Court of Appeals that challenges the District’s felon-in-possession law — is an example of what has become a legal assault on the city’s restrictive gun laws, including litigation around D.C.’s ban on high-powered rifles and high-capacity magazines.

Similar legal challenges have been percolating in courts across the country, and at least one will be heard later this year by the Supreme Court.

Proponents say they’re merely taking the path opened by the Supreme Court in 2008, when it overturned D.C.’s absolute ban on handgun ownership, and later in 2022, when it significantly raised the bar for gun restrictions to comply with the Second Amendment.

“The court has made clear the Second Amendment won’t be treated as a second-class right anymore,” said Clark Neily, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute and attorney who worked on the 2008 case that tossed out D.C.’s handgun ban.

But critics worry that the current litigation, if successful, will usher in an era of even more high-powered guns on the city’s streets, leading to more deaths. (D.C. police estimate that roughly three-quarters of the city’s homicides involve guns. As of September 1, 1,789 illegal guns have been recovered by police in 2026.)

“The weakening of our gun laws is only going to make public safety more difficult,” said D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson.

In some cases, the Trump administration has led the charge against D.C.’s gun laws, while at the same time aggressively pushing to improve public safety in the city.

Last year, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, said her office, which prosecutes most violent crime in the city, would no longer charge people for carrying a rifle or a shotgun or for possessing magazines that can hold more than 10 bullets in them, arguing the laws prohibiting them conflicted with the administration’s pro-gun agenda and were likely unconstitutional.

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb has argued the ban helps prevent mass casualties when shootings happen. But earlier this year, a panel of judges on the D.C. Court of Appeals disagreed with him, declaring that the city’s ban on high-capacity magazines is unconstitutional.

The Trump administration has also sued D.C. over its ban on AR-15 assault rifles, calling it an unconstitutional infringement of the Second Amendment right of individuals to bear arms.

Both that case and further appeals in litigation involving high-capacity magazines are now on hold, because the Supreme Court is scheduled to hear a case later this year involving similar bans on assault rifles across the country.

Much of this litigation has stemmed from the Supreme Court’s 2022 Bruen decision, which says only gun restrictions that have some equivalent in American history or tradition can survive constitutional scrutiny.

“We saw an absolute explosion of litigation in the wake of the Bruen decision, where the governing standard for the Second Amendment claims was rejected and the court announced this new history and tradition test,” said Billy Clark, the associate litigation director at the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence.

The Bruen decision has been cited in challenges to D.C.’s ban on high-capacity magazines, and it’s the central argument in Redman’s appeal of his conviction for possessing a gun as a felon. “There is no historical precedent for permanently disarming a person based solely on a past conviction for a crime punishable by more than one year in prison,” his public defenders argued in a brief to the Court of Appeals this month.

Since Pirro’s office prosecuted Redman, it will be left to them to decide whether to defend D.C.’s felon-in-possession law. “U.S. Attorney Pirro will always fight to keep illegal firearms out of the hands of dangerous felons,” a spokesperson said in an email.

The issue may also be destined for the Supreme Court, though, as multiple federal courts have split on whether felons should be banned from owning guns. Neily said he could see a ruling, whether from the Supreme Court or the D.C. Court of Appeals, that keeps some restrictions in place while tossing out a categorical ban.

“If you just say ‘felon in possession’ you think of a scary person who stuck up a liquor store, and it’s not hard to think they should not have a gun,” he said. “But there’s a guy in Pennsylvania who was convicted of food stamp fraud in the mid-1990s, never went to jail, and is prohibited from owning a gun for life. That’s bonkers.”

In Redman’s case, his initial felony charge in D.C. was for carrying a gun without a license. But he’s also facing armed robbery and assault charges in Maryland.

For Mendelson, the arguments against D.C.’s gun laws fail to capture the real issues facing cities struggling to keep residents safe.

“I don’t believe the founding fathers had a scintilla of thought of semi-automatic pistols or automatic weapons or felons in possession,” he told NOTUS. “They were thinking of muskets. Really, George Washington would travel some of our streets and say this is OK?”
